name: Anansi
culture_or_origin: Akan storytelling traditions; also told across West Africa and the Caribbean
description: A spider storyteller whose clever moves shape tales across Akan and Caribbean traditions. Anansi can win through resourcefulness, but the stories do not always reward every scheme.

sources.title: Ananse — Folktale and Fairy Tale Resources

name: Br'er Rabbit
culture_or_origin: African American and African diaspora folktale traditions
description: A small animal protagonist who repeatedly outthinks stronger opponents. The appeal of these tales lies in how a vulnerable character survives through imagination rather than force.

sources.title: Animal and Trickster Tales — American Folklife Center

name: Coyote (selected traditions)
culture_or_origin: Several distinct Indigenous storytelling traditions of North America
description: Coyote features in stories shared by different Native communities, often upsetting expectations through unconventional choices. Those traditions have distinct voices and should not be collapsed into a single version.

sources.publisher: National Museum of the American Indian
sources.title: Cherokee Days: Storyteller Robert Lewis

name: Èṣù (Eshu)
description: A divine messenger associated with thresholds, crossroads and the possibility of change. Describing Èṣù solely as a prankster would flatten a much broader spiritual role.

sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Museum of African Art
sources.title: Staff — Èṣù (Eshu or Elegba)

name: Hermes
description: The Greek messenger of the gods is also associated with travelers and movement between worlds. Stories about his ingenuity and deception give this boundary-crossing deity a trickster dimension.

name: Loki
description: Loki is both a source of crises among the Norse gods and an occasional solver of their problems. His shapechanging and verbal ingenuity make the line between help and trouble difficult to hold.

name: Māui
culture_or_origin: Māori traditions within the wider Polynesian world
description: Māui's daring feats in Māori stories include bringing islands from the sea and capturing the sun. He is a culture hero whose audacity does more than simply create mischief.

sources.publisher: Te Ara — Encyclopedia of New Zealand
sources.title: First peoples in Māori tradition

name: Nasreddin Hodja
culture_or_origin: Shared anecdote traditions across Azerbaijan, Central Asia and Türkiye
description: In anecdotes carried across multiple communities, Nasreddin uses a surprising reply or upside-down solution to expose an assumption. The fool and the teacher can sound remarkably alike.

name: Raven (Tlingit storytelling)
description: In a Tlingit account of the world's light, Raven transforms himself and tricks his way toward releasing celestial lights. This entry presents one documented tradition, not every Raven narrative.

sources.publisher: National Museum of the American Indian
sources.title: How Raven Stole the Sun

name: Reynard the Fox
culture_or_origin: Medieval European beast epics, especially French and Low Countries traditions
description: The eloquent fox of medieval beast narratives repeatedly turns a world of stronger animals to his advantage. His exploits became a way to mock institutions and displays of power.

name: Sun Wukong (Monkey King)
culture_or_origin: Chinese literary tradition, notably Journey to the West
description: The Monkey King of Journey to the West changes form, resists authority and seeks freedom from limits. His fantastic abilities make him both an unruly figure and a formidable traveling companion.

sources.title: The history behind Sun Wukong, China's Monkey King
